title: High Court bars Kolkata civic poll notice until Friday as it weighs 209-ward map
dek: A Division Bench has reserved its order on a challenge to the redrawing of Kolkata's wards from 144 to 209, and recorded that no election notification will be issued before 6 November.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Calcutta High Court on Wednesday stopped the state from notifying elections to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) until at least Friday, 6 November, while it decides an appeal against the redrawing of the city's wards from 144 to 209.

A vacation Division Bench reserved its order on the appeal and recorded an interim restraint on issuing any notification calling KMC elections on the basis of the disputed delimitation notification until 6 November, reports said. The State had asked the court not to pass an order, and the bench instead sought an assurance that no notification would be issued in the meantime. According to another report, the bench said the State Election Commission (SEC) should not announce the poll schedule until the verdict.

## Wednesday's hearing

The appeal was filed by the petitioner who lost his plea for an interim stay before a single judge last week; a Bengali news site identified him as Dipu Das, a CPI(M) member from Kasba. Senior advocate Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya argued that the KMC's Administrator could not exercise the powers of an elected corporation, especially as she is an employee of the corporation, and that the exercise amounted to gerrymandering. The KMC's elected board was dissolved on 8 June and the corporation has since been run by an Administrator.

Advocate General Surajit Nath Mitra, for the State, said the government did not need the approval of an elected council, that the Administrator held all the corporation's powers, and that Article 243ZG of the Constitution allows delimitation to be questioned only through an election petition after polls. He told the court that the election process had not begun. Counsel for the SEC said it had no information on when the elections would be notified, as that rests with the State.

The bench said it was considering only whether action based on the notification should be stayed. It observed, prima facie, that an elected corporation's powers could not be vested in an Administrator, and that because the KMC Act requires the State to act on the corporation's recommendation, if the Administrator could exercise those powers "the State Government is giving an instruction to itself", one report said.

## The single judge's order

Last week a single judge of the High Court refused to stay the redrawing of the wards, which would have left the State Election Commission free to hold the KMC elections on the new map.

Justice Hiranmay Bhattacharyya declined to suspend a state notification dated September 11 that amended the KMC Act to set out the 209 wards, finding no prima facie case for interim relief, according to reports. The judge said the "balance of convenience and inconvenience is against passing of any interim order", and that a stay would affect the interest of the public at large. The order was passed on Thursday, October 29; one report said that the matter was heard the day before.

## The challenge

The petition was filed by a resident of the city and argued by senior advocate Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya. It asked the court to declare the whole exercise void.

According to the reports, the petitioner argued that the wards had been drawn on the basis of electoral rolls rather than actual population, so that some residents were left out, and that the boundaries ignored geographical contiguity, compactness and administrative convenience. One report said that the petition also alleged the boundaries were shaped by previous election results to benefit the ruling party. The petitioner further argued that the KMC had already been dissolved when the change was recommended, so the Municipal Commissioner, as an officer of the corporation, had no power to recommend it under the KMC Act, 1980.

Advocate General Surajit Nath Mitra, appearing for the KMC, argued that the petition was not maintainable because Article 243ZG of the Constitution bars courts from interfering in the delimitation of municipal wards. He told the court that the Municipal Commissioner had been appointed Administrator on June 8 with all the powers of the corporation's elected members, that objections had been invited and heard in stages, and that the petitioner had filed none.

## What the court decided

The judge agreed to hear the petition on limited grounds because no election notification has yet been issued, but held that, at this stage, the challenge could cover only whether objections were invited and hearings given. He found that the Administrator was competent to recommend the change and that the state has the power to amend the schedule of wards. He said the petitioner "cannot be allowed to take a stand at this point of time" after not filing objections, reports said.

The court made clear that its findings are only prima facie. The allegations about population and partisanship will be examined at the final hearing.

## Background

The process began with a notice on August 5 inviting objections to a draft schedule of wards. The KMC (Amendment) Act, 2026 came into force on August 20, objections were accepted from August 22 to September 3, and the final notification followed on September 11, according to reports. The KMC has been run by an administrator since June. One report noted that the law requires elections within six months of dissolution, and the court said a stay would leave the city without elected councillors for longer.

## The appeal

On Monday, 2 November, the petitioner moved a Calcutta High Court Division Bench against the single judge's refusal of an interim stay, seeking urgent hearing and relief on the ground that the plea would become infructuous once the election schedule is announced, one report said. The bench of Justice Arindam Mukherjee declined immediate relief but allowed the petitioner to file the appeal, observing that because the case was already admitted by the single judge the applicant could approach the court at any stage, even after elections are announced. The same report said elections to the Kolkata and Howrah municipal corporations may be held between late November and early December, and that opposition parties raised the delimitation and the ongoing Special Intensive Revision at a recent all-party meeting.

## What happens next

The Division Bench is due to deliver its order on Friday, 6 November. If it upholds the single judge's refusal, the State Election Commission will be free to announce the KMC poll on the 209-ward map; if it stays the delimitation, the poll timetable could slip. One report said that elections to seven urban bodies in the state, including Kolkata, are likely in December, though no date has been announced.

The reports differ on the timetable for the case. Two reports said the respondents must file affidavits within three weeks, with the petitioner replying a week later. A news agency, in a report carried by a Hindi daily, said the state has four weeks and the petitioner two weeks after that, with the case to be listed again after six weeks. No reactions from political parties to the order had been reported by Saturday morning.
